table.text: Participants were recruited through university SONA systems, campus-wide emails, and flyers.

Participants were screened for exclusion (e.g., presence of cardiac pacemaker, diagnosis of hypertension, medications with cardiac side effects) and inclusion criteria (e.g., at least 18 years old, with a romantic partner, best friend, or stranger, as applicable).
Physiological sensors were then affixed to record cardiovascular responses, and participants were instructed to sit quietly while a 5-minute resting baseline was collected.

After instructions, but prior to the conversation, participants were given 3 minutes to gather their thoughts on the upcoming discussion topic and complete a short questionnaire assessing perceived resources and demands.
Following completion of the study, participants were debriefed and compensated.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The data reported here were part of individual projects examining cardiovascular markers of challenge and threat during social interactions spanning 2012-2025. A priori power analyses conducted for these studies are reported elsewhere (Study 1, Peters et al., 2014; Peters & Jamieson, 2016; Study 2, Peters et al., 2018; Study 3, Peters et al., 2024; Study 4, Tudder et al., 2023; Gresham et al., 2023). In the smallest of these samples, given an averaged effect size (r = .26) from dyadic emotion regulation studies that included physiological measures at the time (2012) of data collection and a target power level of .80, 45 dyads were needed in each experimental condition, totaling 90 dyads (Peters et al., 2014).

table.title: Self-Reported and Physiological Measures of Challenge and Threat Across Social Contexts
table.design_dependent_variables:
INDEPENDENT VARIABLES: 

Conversation role: Across studies, one dyad member (the discloser) was tasked with either disclosing hypothetical good news to their partner, identifying the top three pet peeves they have of their partner or the top three ways they depend on their partner, or disclosing their most stressful ongoing issue that did not involve their interaction partner. The other person (the responder) either received no additional instruction or was informed that the discloser would be disclosing some information or going first. Thus, across all studies, dyad members could be distinguished by this variable (-1 = responder, 1 = discloser).

Conversation condition: For two of the three studies pre-registered here, a portion of the topic of conversation was randomly assigned as an experimental condition. In one (CGN), dyads were given a hypothetical situation in which they would either be able to live together or be forced to live 1000 miles apart. For the other (PEB), dyads were either told to discuss their top three pet peeves about their partner or the top three ways they depend upon their partner. Thus, where applicable, conversation condition was examined (CGN: -1 = together, 1 = apart; PEB: -1 = pet peeves, 1 = dependence). 

Self-reported appraisals: Participants self-reported perceived demands and available resources in anticipation of the conversation as well as after the interaction’s conclusion. In one study, self-reported appraisals were also collected retrospectively in reference to each individual minute of the conversation. These appraisals were measured through responses to two items assessing resources (“I have the abilities to do well during the conversation”/ “I felt I had the abilities to do well during the situation”; “I’m the kind of person who does well with these types of conversations”/ “I believe I did well in this part of the conversation”), and two assessing demands (“The upcoming conversation is demanding”/ “The conversation was very demanding”; “The upcoming conversation will take a lot of effort to complete”/ “I exerted a lot of effort during this part of the conversation”). Each item was rated on a Likert-type scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree), and a self-reported challenge-threat index will be created by taking the difference of resources and demands such that higher scores indicate greater challenge and less threat (Behnke & Kaczmarek, 2018; Beltzer et al., 2014; Mendes et al., 2007b; Seery, 2011).

DEPENDENT VARIABLES: 

Cardiovascular reactivity: Cardiovascular signals (Pre-ejection period (PEP), cardiac output (CO), and total peripheral resistance (TPR)) were recorded during baseline and before, during, and after each conversation using electrocardiography (ECG), impedance cardiography (ICG), and blood pressure cuffs. Reactivity scores (PEP, CO, and TPR) were then computed by subtracting scores obtained during the last minute of baseline from those obtained during the first minute of a target task (i.e., anticipation, conversation, or recovery). Note, for one study (PEB), the conversation was segmented into four parts, creating up to four target task variables to assess during the conversation for that study. PEP was calculated as the time between Q and B-points across the ECG and dZ/dt wave from each minute. CO was calculated using the product of stroke volume (the volume of blood ejected by the heart per beat; computed using the Kubicek equation via Mindware analytic software) and heart rate. TPR was derived from dividing MAP by CO and multiplying this value by 80. A physiological challenge-threat index will be created by standardizing CO and TPR and taking the difference of CO and TPR such that higher scores indicated greater challenge and less threat.
table.study_design_overview: See above ​(under independent variables) ​for description of conversation role and condition.
table.statistical_tests:
A series of multilevel models will be conducted in SPSS 29 using the MIXED procedure. Following guidelines by Kenny et al. (2006), analyses will account for the non-independence of cases inherent in dyadic data collection. Participants within a dyad were distinguished by their role in the conversation (discloser vs. responder) or sex (male vs. female). Before testing our hypotheses, PEP scores from the first minute of each time period (anticipation, conversation, and recovery) will be compared to scores from the last minute of the baseline data collection period. Through this analysis we can determine if PEP reactivity within each time period differs significantly from zero, indicating sympathetic arousal and task engagement (Johnston et al., 2022). 

To test our first hypothesis, that greater scores on the self-reported challenge-threat index would be associated with greater scores on the physiological challenge-threat index, we will regress our dependent variable (physiological challenge-threat index) on the fixed effect of the self-reported challenge-threat index. To test our exploratory research question regarding conversation role and conversation condition as moderators of the association between the self-reported and physiological challenge-threat indices, we will enter the following fixed effects as applicable: role (-1 = responder, 1 = discloser), condition (CGN: -1 = together, 1 = apart; PEB: -1 = pet peeves, 1 = dependence), all possible two-way interaction terms with the self-reported challenge-threat index, role, and condition, as well as the three-way interaction.

As self-reported appraisals and physiological recordings were collected at multiple time points throughout the study (anticipation, conversation, and recovery periods), analyses will be conducted for each theoretically consistent test of the association between self-reported appraisals and cardiovascular reactivity (i.e., anticipation period appraisals predicting cardiovascular reactivity during the anticipation period, anticipation period appraisals predicting cardiovascular reactivity during the conversation, recovery period appraisals predicting cardiovascular reactivity during the conversation, and recovery period appraisals predicting cardiovascular reactivity during the recovery period). However, the primary test will be anticipation period appraisals predicting cardiovascular reactivity during the conversation.

In one study (FIRE), participants reviewed footage of their completed conversation and retrospectively self-reported perceived resources and demands for each minute of the conversation. This design maps self-reported appraisals onto cardiovascular reactivity on a minute-by-minute basis during the conversation task. Additionally, dyadic, repeated-measures data allows us to model covariation at the within- and between-person level (Bolger & Laurenceau, 2013). Specifically, this dataset has the advantage of allowing for analyses examining the person-to-person variation in how strongly within-person differences in self-reported appraisals are associated with cardiovascular reactivity.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Physiological data from these studies have been cleaned and reported as part of prior publications. Physiological outliers were previously identified and corrected (in the case of a typo or mistake) or removed (machine error, noisy signals). ​​​​​​​Self-reported data was excluded if participants responded incorrectly to inattention checks (e.g., “click ‘3’ for this answer”).
table.sample_size: The 3 of 5 datasets as part of this pre-registration use data from approximately 872 individuals in 436 dyads.
table.additional_comments: Previous publications (Girme et al., 2021; Peters et al., 2018, 2024; Shimshock et al., 2024; Tudder et al., 2020) have utilized these datasets. However, the association between self-reported appraisals and cardiovascular reactivity was not examined in any of the aforementioned work. Thus, the proposed work is distinct and has not been previously examined.
table.name: Self-Reported and Physiological Measures of Challenge and Threat Across Social Contexts
table.data_collection_started: It's complicated. We have already collected some data but explain in Question 8 why readers may consider this a valid pre-registration nevertheless.
table.research_questions:
Research Question: To what extent are self-reports indexing challenge and threat states associated with cardiovascular responses indicative of challenge and threat states?

(H1) Self-reports indicative of greater challenge (and less threat) will be associated with cardiovascular reactivity that indexes greater challenge (and less threat) (i.e., a main effect). 

Exploratory Research Question: To what extent is the association between self-reported and physiological indicators of challenge and threat moderated by conversation role and (as applicable) experimental condition?

Note: The three datasets pre-registered here are part of a larger, five-study project (internal study names: EES, CRR/FRR, CGN, PEB, FIRE). The current hypotheses were not pre-registered for one of these datasets (EES). A prior pre-registration of a second dataset (CRR/FRR) hypothesized a three-way interaction (appraisal × role × condition), but no evidence of this interaction was found. As a result, analyses on the remaining three datasets pre-registered here (CGN, PEB, FIRE) will treat the moderation of role and condition as an exploratory research question.

These research questions will be primarily tested using self-reported appraisals collected during the anticipation period predicting cardiovascular responses obtained during the conversation. In addition to this, we will conduct exploratory analyses on all other relevant time combinations (i.e., anticipation period appraisals predicting cardiovascular reactivity during the anticipation period, recovery period appraisals predicting cardiovascular reactivity during the conversation, and recovery period appraisals predicting cardiovascular reactivity during the recovery period). Additionally, one dataset (FIRE) allows us to examine the association between self-reported appraisals and cardiovascular reactivity on a minute-by-minute basis during the conversation task, and consequently between- and within-person differences will be assessed.

table.title: Self-Reported and Physiological Measures of Challenge and Threat during Co-Rumination
table.design_dependent_variables:
INDEPENDENT VARIABLES: 

Role: (-1 = responder, 1 = discloser). One individual within a dyad was randomly assigned to disclose their most stressful ongoing issue that did not involve their interaction partner. The other person was informed that the discloser would be disclosing information and going first.

Condition: (-1 = natural, 1 = co-rumination). Dyads were randomly assigned to either the co-rumination or natural condition. In the co-rumination condition, participants were instructed to stay on topic, go over the problem multiple times, speculate about the causes and consequences of the problem, and uncover and dig into negative emotions. Dyads in the natural condition were instructed to engage in discussion as they naturally would. Participants in both conditions were given cards to remind them of their instructions during the discussion. 

Self-Reported Appraisals: Participants self-reported perceived demands and available resources in anticipation of the support discussion as well as after the interaction’s conclusion. These were measured through responses to two items assessing resource appraisals (“I have the abilities to do well during the conversation”/ “I felt I had the abilities to do well during the situation”; “I’m the kind of person who does well with these types of conversations”/ “I believe I did well in this part of the conversation”), and two assessing demand appraisals (“The upcoming conversation is demanding”/ “The conversation was very demanding”; “The upcoming conversation will take a lot of effort to complete”/ “I exerted a lot of effort during this part of the conversation”). Each item was rated on a Likert-type scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree), and a self-report challenge-threat index was created by taking the difference of resources and demands such that higher scores indicated greater challenge and less threat (Behnke & Kaczmarek, 2018; Beltzer et al., 2014; Mendes et al., 2007b; Seery, 2011).

Relationship Type (-1 = friends, 1 = romantic partners) Dyads in the sample were either close friends or romantic partners. Analyses will control for the nature of the dyad’s relationship by adding in relationship type as a fixed effect. 

DEPENDENT VARIABLES: 

Physiological Reactivity: Cardiovascular signals (Pre-ejection period (PEP), cardiac output (CO), and total peripheral resistance (TPR)) were recorded during baseline and before, during, and after each conversation using electrocardiography (ECG), impedance cardiography (ICG), and blood pressure cuffs. Reactivity scores (PEP, CO, and TPR) were then computed by subtracting scores obtained during the last minute of baseline from those obtained during the first minute of a target task (i.e., anticipation, conversation, or recovery). PEP was calculated as the time between Q and B-points across the ECG and dZ/dt wave from each minute. CO was calculated using the product of stroke volume (the volume of blood ejected by the heart per beat; computed using the Kubicek equation via Mindware analytic software) and heart rate. TPR was derived from dividing MAP by CO and multiplying this value by 80. A physiological challenge-threat index was created by standardizing CO and TPR and taking the difference of CO and TPR such that higher scores indicated greater challenge and less threat.

table.statistical_tests:
A series of multilevel models will be conducted in SPSS 29 using the MIXED procedure. Following guidelines by Kenny et al. (2006), analyses will account for the non-independence of cases inherent in dyadic data collection. In these analyses, we will also control for the nature of the dyad’s relationship by adding in relationship type as a fixed effect (-1 = friends, 1 = romantic partners). Participants within a dyad will be distinguished by their role in the conversation (discloser vs. responder). Before testing our hypotheses, PEP scores from the first minute of each time period (anticipation, conversation, and recovery) will be compared to scores from the last minute of the baseline data collection period. Through this analysis we can determine if PEP reactivity within each time period differs significantly from zero, indicating sympathetic arousal and task engagement (Johnston et al., 2022).

To test our first hypothesis that greater scores on the self-reported challenge-threat index would be associated with greater scores on the physiological challenge-threat index we will regress our dependent variable (physiological challenge-threat index) on the fixed effect of the self-report challenge-threat index. To test our second hypothesis that the association between the self-report and physiological challenge-threat indices would be moderated by experimental condition and role in the conversation, we will enter the following fixed effects: condition (-1 = natural, 1 = co-rumination), role (-1 = responder, 1 = discloser), all possible two-way interaction terms with self-report challenge-threat index, condition, and role, as well as the three-way interaction. As self-reported appraisals and physiological recordings were collected at multiple time points throughout the study (self-reported appraisals were collected during anticipation and recovery periods; physiological reactivity was collected during anticipation, conversation, and recovery periods), analyses will be conducted for each theoretically consistent test of the association between appraisals and physiological reactivity (i.e., anticipation period appraisals predicting physiological reactivity during the anticipation period, anticipation period appraisals predicting physiological reactivity during the conversation, recovery period appraisals predicting physiological reactivity during the conversation, and recovery period appraisals predicting physiological reactivity during the recovery period). However, the primary test will be anticipation period appraisals predicting physiological reactivity during the conversation.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Physiological data from these studies have been cleaned and reported as part of prior publications. Physiological outliers were previously identified and corrected (in the case of a typo or mistake) or removed (machine error, noisy signals). ​​​​​​​Self-reported data was excluded if participants responded incorrectly to inattention checks (e.g., “click ‘3’ for this answer”).
table.sample_size: The sample consisted of 610 individuals (405 females, 203 males, 2 others; Mage = 19.53, SD = 1.30, range = 18–30 years) making up 305 dyads. Prior to data collection, a series of Monte Carlo simulations were conducted with equality constraints for paths modeling effects of each dyad (Lane & Hennes, 2018; Mehl & Conner, 2012) with the use of past dyadic datasets to approximate effects (Peters & Jamieson, 2016; Peters et al., 2014, 2019; Tudder et al., 2020). Focusing on a small to medium effect size (r ~ .15), it was determined that 120 dyads were needed to achieve sufficient power (> .80) for a three-way interaction effect. Following recruitment of the minimum target sample size, data collection continued through the end of the academic year.
table.additional_comments: The friendship sample has been used in past research to examine physiological synchrony (DiGiovanni et al., 2024), challenge and threat reactivity (Lang et al., 2024; Tudder et al., 2023), and behavioral synchrony (Lin et al., 2023). The relationship sample has been used in past research to examine anticipatory stress appraisals on behavior (Peters et al., 2024), relational power and physiological response, and physiological synchrony (DiGiovanni et al., 2024). However, the association between self-reported appraisals and physiological reactivity was not examined in any of the aforementioned work. Thus, the proposed work is distinct and has not been examined before.

table.data_collection_started: It's complicated. We have already collected some data but explain in Question 8 why readers may consider this a valid pre-registration nevertheless.
table.research_questions:
Research Question: To what extent are self-reports indexing challenge and threat states associated with cardiovascular responses indicative of challenge and threat states?

(H1) Self-reports indicative of greater challenge (and less threat) will be associated with cardiovascular reactivity that indexes greater challenge (and less threat) (i.e., a main effect). 

(H2) This positive association between appraisals and cardiovascular reactivity will be moderated by role and experimental condition, such that the association between self-report and physio will be strengthened for those who were told to disclose their problems and co-ruminate (an interaction of appraisal × role  × condition).

These hypotheses will be primarily tested using self-reported appraisals collected during the anticipation period predicting cardiovascular responses obtained during the conversation. In addition to this, we will conduct exploratory analyses on all other relevant time combinations (i.e., anticipation period appraisals predicting cardiovascular reactivity during the anticipation period, recovery period appraisals predicting cardiovascular reactivity during the conversation, and recovery period appraisals predicting cardiovascular reactivity during the recovery period.)

Conversation role: Across studies, one dyad member (the discloser) was tasked with either disclosing hypothetical good news to their partner, identifying the top three pet peeves they have of their partner or the top three ways they depend on their partner, or disclosing their most stressful ongoing issue that did not involve their interaction partner. The other person (the responder) either received no additional instruction or was informed that the discloser would be disclosing some information or going first. Thus, across all studies, dyad members could be distinguished by this variable (-1 = responder, 1 = discloser).

Conversation condition: For two of the three studies pre-registered here, a portion of the topic of conversation was randomly assigned as an experimental condition. In one (CGN), dyads were given a hypothetical situation in which they would either be able to live together or be forced to live 1000 miles apart. For the other (PEB), dyads were either told to discuss their top three pet peeves about their partner or the top three ways they depend upon their partner. Thus, where applicable, conversation condition was examined (CGN: -1 = together, 1 = apart; PEB: -1 = pet peeves, 1 = dependence).

Self-reported appraisals: Participants self-reported perceived demands and available resources in anticipation of the conversation as well as after the interaction’s conclusion. In one study, self-reported appraisals were also collected retrospectively in reference to each individual minute of the conversation. These appraisals were measured through responses to two items assessing resources (“I have the abilities to do well during the conversation”/ “I felt I had the abilities to do well during the situation”; “I’m the kind of person who does well with these types of conversations”/ “I believe I did well in this part of the conversation”), and two assessing demands (“The upcoming conversation is demanding”/ “The conversation was very demanding”; “The upcoming conversation will take a lot of effort to complete”/ “I exerted a lot of effort during this part of the conversation”). Each item was rated on a Likert-type scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree), and a self-reported challenge-threat index will be created by taking the difference of resources and demands such that higher scores indicate greater challenge and less threat (Behnke & Kaczmarek, 2018; Beltzer et al., 2014; Mendes et al., 2007b; Seery, 2011).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .487", "p = .959", "p = .949"), Sentence = c("In Study 5, we did not find evidence that the selfreported indices of individuals who reported feeling more challenged than they typically felt during the conversation were associated with cardiovascular indices of greater challenge and less threat (i.e., no within-person effect; B = .02, SE = .03, t = 0.70, p = .487, r = .08, BF01 = 1.18e+12).", "Both the fixed effects test (M r = -.001, Z = -.052, p = .959, twotailed; see Figure 1) and the random effects test (M r = .001, t = .067, p = .949, two-tailed; see Figure 2; Sibley, 2008) were not significant.", "Both the fixed effects test (M r = -.001, Z = -.052, p = .959, twotailed; see Figure 1) and the random effects test (M r = .001, t = .067, p = .949, two-tailed; see Figure 2; Sibley, 2008) were not significant." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. table.column_name: Fixed and random effects meta-analysis of studies using r-effect sizes
table.sample_values: This excel file calculates meta-analytic averages and associated tests for r. Enter independent r-effect sizes and the corresponding N for each sample in the columns | below. The top box reports average z values and average values transformed back into original r metric assuming a fixed-effects model. The lower box calculates | meta-analytic averages assuming a random effects variance component (v0) using a non-iterative method of moments approach. For an excellent and | very accessible introduction to the meta-analytic procedures used here, as well as more complex weighed ANOVA and weighed regression analyses | see Lipsey and Wilson (2001). A calculator for the simple (ANOVA equivalent) test of between-groups differences in effect size is also provided.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 3074 columns across 46 data files.
#### Issues Identified

178 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 46 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants were recruited through university SONA systems, campus-wide emails, and flyers.

Participants were screened for exclusion (e.g., presence of cardiac pacemaker, diagnosis of hypertension, medications with cardiac side effects) and inclusion criteria (e.g., at least 18 years old, with a romantic partner, best friend, or stranger, as applicable).
Physiological sensors were then affixed to record cardiovascular responses, and participants were instructed to sit quietly while a 5-minute resting baseline was collected.

After instructions, but prior to the conversation, participants were given 3 minutes to gather their thoughts on the upcoming discussion topic and complete a short questionnaire assessing perceived resources and demands.
Following completion of the study, participants were debriefed and compensated.

info.title: **THIS ARTICLE HAS BEEN CONDITIONALLY ACCEPTED AND HAS NOT YET BEEN PUBLISHED** A mind-body disconnection? Discordance between thoughts about stress and cardiovascular stress responses

text.text: Stress responses are defined by mind-body interactions that engage both psychological and physiological processes.
We provide foundational research investigating the mind-body connection during stress to ask: how do individuals' thoughts about stressors align with their cardiovascular responses?
925 dyads (N = 1,850) anticipated, engaged in, and recovered from stress-inducing social-evaluative tasks.

Analyses revealed that individuals' self-reported and cardiovascular indices of stress were not significantly associated at any timepoint, bolstered by post-hoc Inclusion Bayes Factors supporting the null (vs. alternative) hypothesis.

Meta-analytic results suggested the association between measures is effectively zero, indicating findings may generalize beyond a social interaction context and our primarily White, female, college-aged sample.

These findings suggest individuals' perceptions of stress may be distinct from their physiological stress responses, carry significant implications for the way we conceptualize and measure stress, and indicate that multi-method, full-body approaches are critical for a holistic understanding of the human stress response.

text.text: The concept of the "mind-body connection" is a foundational one, spurring research across science and health for years.
Stress, a ubiquitous part of life, illustrates this connection, as physiological responses are influenced by and shape perception to drive behavior.

Indeed, many theoretical models conceptualize stress as a "full-body" experience, recognizing that actively responding to stress engages a wide range of systems above and beyond any single process (e.g., McEwen, 2013; Blascovich & Mendes, 2001).
text.formatted: Indeed, many theoretical models conceptualize stress as a "full-body" experience, recognizing that actively responding to stress engages a wide range of systems above and beyond any single process (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">McEwen, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Blascovich & Mendes, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Despite this acknowledgement, the field currently lacks a comprehensive understanding of how conscious perception and physiological responses cohere in the face of stress.
Under what conditions do the mind and body align or diverge in their responses?
Elucidating these patterns provides a foundational step towards predicting and managing stress-related outcomes.

The Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT) provides a comprehensive framework of the psychological and physiological processes underlying stress responses (Blascovich & Tomaka, 1996; Blascovich & Mendes, 2010).
text.formatted: The Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT) provides a comprehensive framework of the psychological and physiological processes underlying stress responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Blascovich & Tomaka, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Blascovich & Mendes, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Within potentially stressful contexts, the BPS-CT posits that an individual appraises the ability of their available resources (e.g., support, abilities, knowledge) to meet the demands (e.g., effort, uncertainty, potential danger) of the situation.
When resources meet or exceed demands, a state of greater challenge is induced, whereas when demands exceed resources, a state of greater threat is induced.

Resource and demand appraisals are typically self-reported individually before being combined into a single-score index, which extant work has validated as a measure of underlying states of challenge and threat (e.g., Mendes et al., 2007; Beltzer et al., 2014; Peters et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Resource and demand appraisals are typically self-reported individually before being combined into a single-score index, which extant work has validated as a measure of underlying states of challenge and threat (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Mendes et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Beltzer et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Peters et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These psychological challenge and threat states can also be indexed through patterns of cardiovascular changes in the body (measured as reactivity relative to a resting baseline; Seery, 2011).
text.formatted: These psychological challenge and threat states can also be indexed through patterns of cardiovascular changes in the body (measured as reactivity relative to a resting baseline; <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Seery, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In a state of greater challenge and less threat, the body responds by supplying resources to the periphery to quickly cope with a stressor (Blascovich & Mendes, 2001 , 2010).
text.formatted: In a state of greater challenge and less threat, the body responds by supplying resources to the periphery to quickly cope with a stressor <ref type="bibr">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2001</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, a state of greater threat and less challenge is associated with a more prolonged physiological stress response in anticipation of potential defeat.
Two cardiovascular measures (cardiac output [CO] and total peripheral resistance [TPR]) are collected and often combined into a single index (e.g., Johnston et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Two cardiovascular measures (cardiac output <ref type="bibr">[CO]</ref> and total peripheral resistance <ref type="bibr">[TPR]</ref>) are collected and often combined into a single index (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Johnston et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Extant work has demonstrated the ability of this cardiovascular index to predict theory-consistent outcomes of stress (e.g., Hangen et al., 2016; Chin & Feeney, 2022).
text.formatted: Extant work has demonstrated the ability of this cardiovascular index to predict theory-consistent outcomes of stress (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Hangen et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Chin & Feeney, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the BPS-CT conceptualizes the mind and body as interconnected systems that inform one another to drive stress responses.
Both self-reported and cardiovascular indices have been used extensively, but often separately, to examine stress through the lens of the BPS-CT.

For example, the relation between a greater challenge state and better performance across cognitive, athletic, and social-evaluative domains has been well-supported by both self-report (for reviews, see Hase et al., 2019; 2025) and cardiovascular measures (for a review, see Behnke & Kaczmarek, 2018).
text.formatted: For example, the relation between a greater challenge state and better performance across cognitive, athletic, and social-evaluative domains has been well-supported by both self-report (for reviews, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hase et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">2025)</ref> and cardiovascular measures (for a review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Behnke & Kaczmarek, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, some studies implementing both operationalizations have revealed divergent patterns (e.g., Turner et al., 2013; Gresham et al., 2023; Lang et al., 2024), raising questions about the relation between psychological and cardiovascular stress responses.
text.formatted: However, some studies implementing both operationalizations have revealed divergent patterns (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Turner et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Gresham et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Lang et al., 2024)</ref>, raising questions about the relation between psychological and cardiovascular stress responses.

text.text: To make sense of when and why these measures may converge or diverge in predicting outcomes of stress, we first need to know the extent to which these indices of stress are associated with one another.
However, a review of the literature provides mixed evidence of an association between the two measures (see Table S1 for a comprehensive overview).
text.formatted: However, a review of the literature provides mixed evidence of an association between the two measures (see Table <ref type="table">S1</ref> for a comprehensive overview).

text.text: Of the extant work, many have not found evidence of a significant association between self-reported and cardiovascular patterns, some have reported associations with contradictory patterns (i.e., self-reported measures indicative of greater threat and less challenge predicting cardiovascular patterns of less threat and greater challenge), while others have found mixed or marginal evidence for the association across tasks and measures (see Table S1).
text.formatted: Of the extant work, many have not found evidence of a significant association between self-reported and cardiovascular patterns, some have reported associations with contradictory patterns (i.e., self-reported measures indicative of greater threat and less challenge predicting cardiovascular patterns of less threat and greater challenge), while others have found mixed or marginal evidence for the association across tasks and measures (see Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>).

text.text: After reviewing the literature, we contend that such mixed evidence of the association between psychological and physiological indices of stress may be due to methodological heterogeneity (see Table S1).
text.formatted: After reviewing the literature, we contend that such mixed evidence of the association between psychological and physiological indices of stress may be due to methodological heterogeneity (see Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>).

text.text: First, operationalizations of self-reported appraisals and cardiovascular reactivity vary widely (see Table S1; Hase et al., 2019).
text.formatted: First, operationalizations of self-reported appraisals and cardiovascular reactivity vary widely (see Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>; <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hase et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Second, elements of study design, such as the temporal ordering of measures and sample size (median N = 53), could be contributing to a prevalence of mixed findings.
Third, it may be that the context in which the stressor is embedded shapes the association between self-reported and physiological stress.

As social interactions have been shown to influence both psychological (e.g., Peters et al., 2024) and physiological (e.g., Mendes et al., 2007) indices of challenge and threat, the current work examines the mind-body connection in the context of dyadic conversations.
text.formatted: As social interactions have been shown to influence both psychological (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Peters et al., 2024)</ref> and physiological (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Mendes et al., 2007)</ref> indices of challenge and threat, the current work examines the mind-body connection in the context of dyadic conversations.

text.text: Prior work has found social stressors to be the most common source of stress in daily life (Wheaton et al., 2012; Almeida, 2002), suggesting a social stress context may be more generalizable than alternative athletic and cognitive performance-based paradigms (see Table S1).
text.formatted: Prior work has found social stressors to be the most common source of stress in daily life <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Wheaton et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Almeida, 2002)</ref>, suggesting a social stress context may be more generalizable than alternative athletic and cognitive performance-based paradigms (see Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>).

text.text: The current research examined the association between two channels of the stress response process: individuals' conscious experience of stress (via self-reported appraisals) and their body's response to stress (via cardiovascular reactivity).
The BPS-CT theorizes that as appraisals shift in response to stress, corresponding physiological changes should be observed.
However, few studies have provided evidence of such coherence, potentially due to heterogeneity in methodological approaches (see Table S1).
text.formatted: However, few studies have provided evidence of such coherence, potentially due to heterogeneity in methodological approaches (see Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>).

text.text: In the current work, we addressed this limitation by taking theoretically and empirically supported approaches to measuring stress.
Our primary aim was to better understand whether, when, and how thoughts about stress cohere with physiological responses.
We analyzed the self-reported and cardiovascular data of five dyadic datasets (925 dyads; 1,850 individuals) spanning a range of social interaction tasks and 13 years of in-person data collection.
We hypothesized that self-reported indices of greater challenge and less threat would be associated with cardiovascular indices of greater challenge and less threat.
A post-hoc mini meta-analysis was conducted using data from the current studies as well as extant work with methodological similarity (see Table S1).
text.formatted: A post-hoc mini meta-analysis was conducted using data from the current studies as well as extant work with methodological similarity (see Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>).

text.text: This analysis aimed to assess the robustness of the relation between self-reported and physiological stress across the broader literature by extending and generalizing our findings beyond social interactions.
Because of methodological similarities, we present the methodology used across all studies but note when specific methodologies differed.
No prior work from these datasets has assessed the association between the self-reported and cardiovascular indices using the operationalizations outlined in the current work.

Correlations between some of the self-reported and physiological variables in Studies 2 and 4 have been reported in prior work (Tudder et al., 2020; Gresham et al., 2023), although the operationalizations of these constructs differ from that of our current work, cardiovascular data from the recovery period have never been analyzed, and prior analyses did not control for relationship type or account for the dependence inherent in dyadic data.
text.formatted: Correlations between some of the self-reported and physiological variables in Studies 2 and 4 have been reported in prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Tudder et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Gresham et al., 2023)</ref>, although the operationalizations of these constructs differ from that of our current work, cardiovascular data from the recovery period have never been analyzed, and prior analyses did not control for relationship type or account for the dependence inherent in dyadic data.

text.text: Thus, the analyses conducted here are novel and have not been reported before.
We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all manipulations, and all measures in the study, following JARS (Appelbaum et al., 2018).

text.text: Additional measures were assessed in this study that are not pertinent to the current work.

Due to the dyadic nature of the data and the potential for individuals to identify themselves and their partner, all data and analysis code are available, but have been separated from identifying information.

text.text: Participants were recruited through university SONA systems, campus-wide emails, and flyers.

Participants were screened for exclusion (e.g., presence of cardiac pacemaker, diagnosis of hypertension, medications with cardiac side effects) and inclusion criteria (e.g., at least 18 years old, with a romantic partner, best friend, or stranger, as applicable).
All participants that were deemed eligible were invited to participate (see Table 1 for participant characteristics across the five studies).

All available data were used and no additional exclusions were made.
All procedures were reviewed and approved by each university's (University of Rochester, Studies 1-3; Ohio University, Studies 4-5) respective Institutional Review Boards.
Upon arrival, dyads were separated into private testing rooms where they provided consent and completed baseline questionnaires.
Physiological sensors were then affixed to record cardiovascular responses, and participants were instructed to sit quietly while a 5-minute resting baseline was collected.
Participants then received instructions for a conversation task.

After instructions, but prior to the conversation, participants were given 3 minutes to gather their thoughts on the upcoming discussion topic and complete a short questionnaire assessing perceived resources and demands.
Then, dyads were brought together and engaged in the conversation task (5-8 minutes).
After the conversation, a recovery period (3 minutes) began where participants self-reported resource and demand appraisals in a private setting.
Cardiovascular signals were recorded before, during, and after each conversation.
Following completion of the study, participants were debriefed and compensated.
In Study 1, participants discussed their thoughts and feelings about a clip they independently viewed from a documentary about the bombing of Hiroshima.
In Study 2, one participant received hypothetical good news that they were hired for their dream job/admitted to their dream graduate school.
For Study 3, participants discussed three things about their partner or relationship.
In Studies 4 and 5, dyads discussed one person's ongoing and stressful problem that did not involve the other person.

Across all studies, each person's role in the conversation was manipulated such that one dyad member was given special instructions or was told to disclose a personal problem first (the "discloser") while the other was not (the "responder").

Participants self-reported resource appraisals through responses to two items prior to ("I have the abilities to do well during the conversation"; "I'm the kind of person who does well with these types of conversations"; α = .631, .589, .804, .696, .633) and following the conversation (i.e., "I felt I had the abilities to do well during the conversation"; "I believe I did well during the conversation"; α = .802, .761, .901, .761, .793).

Similarly, demand appraisals were assessed before ("The upcoming conversation is demanding"; "The upcoming conversation will take a lot of effort to complete"; α = .876, .791, .878, .812, .737) and after each conversation (i.e., "The conversation was very demanding"; "I exerted a lot of effort during the conversation"; α = .725, .662, .865, .816, .704).

These items, considered standard in the field (Mendes et al., 2007), have been used extensively in prior research to assess stress in both social-evaluative (e.g., Jamieson et al., 2012; Mendes et al., 2007) and dyadic (e.g., Beltzer et al., 2014; Mendes et al., 2001) contexts.

text.text: Extant work has demonstrated the utility of these items to predict theory-consistent behavioral outcomes (e.g., Peters et al., 2024; Beltzer et al., 2014; Jamieson et al., 2012), providing predictive validity for the measure as an index of underlying challenge/threat states.

text.text: Additionally, these items index resources and demands as opposed to challenge/threat states, as participants may misconstrue the meaning of "challenge" and "threat" and be less accurate in their self-reported appraisals as a result (i.e., the 2026 Merriam-Webster dictionary defines "challenge" as: "to dispute injustice," "confront or defy boldly," or "formally question legality").

In contrast, the BPS-CT suggests that resources and demands can include any number of factors that an individual believes to be relevant to their situation, thus making these terms more accessible for participants to report (e.g., Blascovich & Mendes, 2010; Mendes et al., 2007).

The difference score approach was used to calculate a self-reported challenge-threat index such that higher scores indicated greater challenge and less threat (M = 2.72, SD = 1.81).
Physiological stress responses were indexed via pre-ejection period (PEP), cardiac output (CO) and total peripheral resistance (TPR) measured relative to an individual's resting baseline.

PEP indicates task engagement via activation of the sympathetic nervous system (SNS; i.e., a "fight-or-flight" response), and has been recognized as a more precise and "pure" measure of SNS activation compared to alternatives like heart rate (e.g., Johnston et al., 2023).
text.formatted: PEP indicates task engagement via activation of the sympathetic nervous system (SNS; i.e., a "fight-or-flight" response), and has been recognized as a more precise and "pure" measure of SNS activation compared to alternatives like heart rate (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Johnston et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: CO and TPR serve as physiological indicators of psychological challenge/threat states.

Psychological states of greater challenge and less threat are characterized by increased cardiac efficiency (increased CO) and dilated peripheral vasculature (decreased TPR; see Blascovich & Mendes, 2001 , 2010).
text.formatted: Psychological states of greater challenge and less threat are characterized by increased cardiac efficiency (increased CO) and dilated peripheral vasculature (decreased TPR; see <ref type="bibr">Blascovich & Mendes, 2001</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, a psychological state of greater threat and less challenge is reflected by reduced cardiac efficiency (decreased or no change in CO) and restricted blood flow (increased TPR).

These physiological indicators were measured via the collection of electrocardiography Reactivity scores (PEP, CO, and TPR) were then computed by subtracting scores obtained during the last minute of baseline from those obtained during the first minute of a target task (i.e., anticipation, conversation, or recovery; see Llabre et al., 1991 for justification for using reactivity scores).
text.formatted: These physiological indicators were measured via the collection of electrocardiography Reactivity scores (PEP, CO, and TPR) were then computed by subtracting scores obtained during the last minute of baseline from those obtained during the first minute of a target task (i.e., anticipation, conversation, or recovery; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Llabre et al., 1991</ref> for justification for using reactivity scores).

text.text: PEP was calculated as the time between Q and B points across the ECG and dZ/dt wave from each minute.
CO was calculated using the product of stroke volume (the volume of blood ejected by the heart per beat; computed using the Kubicek equation via Mindware analytic software) and heart rate.
TPR was derived from dividing MAP by CO and multiplying this value by 80.

A cardiovascular challenge-threat index was created by standardizing CO and TPR and taking the difference of CO and TPR such that higher scores indicated greater challenge and less threat, following a common practice in the field (e.g., Johnston et al., 2023).

text.text: A series of multilevel models were conducted in SPSS 31 using the MIXED procedure.
Following guidelines by Kenny et al. (2006), analyses accounted for the non-independence of cases inherent in dyadic data.
text.formatted: Following guidelines by <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Kenny et al. (2006)</ref>, analyses accounted for the non-independence of cases inherent in dyadic data.

text.text: Specifically, dyads were treated as distinguishable based on their role in the conversation (discloser vs. responder, see supplemental for additional details) or sex assigned at birth (female vs. male).
We used a compound symmetry heterogeneous covariance structure which created separate residual variances for each dyad member and allowed them to correlate.
As applicable (Studies 1 and 4), we also controlled for the nature of the dyad's relationship by adding in relationship type as a fixed effect.
Per the BPS-CT, evidence that the stress response system has been activated is a prerequisite for examining cardiovascular indicators of challenge/threat states (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010).

To test our hypothesis that greater scores on the self-reported challenge-threat index would be associated with greater scores on the cardiovascular challenge-threat index we regressed our dependent variable (cardiovascular challenge-threat index) on the fixed effect of the self-reported challenge-threat index.
These research questions were tested using self-reported appraisals collected during the anticipation period and cardiovascular responses obtained during the subsequent conversation.

In addition to these primary analyses, we conducted exploratory tests using other relevant time pairings, including anticipation period appraisals predicting cardiovascular reactivity during the anticipation period, recovery period appraisals predicting cardiovascular reactivity during the conversation, and recovery period appraisals predicting cardiovascular reactivity during the recovery period.
Additionally, one dataset (Study 5) enabled a more granular examination of the relation between self-reported and cardiovascular indices on a minute-by-minute basis during the conversation task.
This allowed us to assess both betweenand within-person associations as the conversation unfolded.

In order to interpret CO and TPR as cardiovascular markers of psychological challenge and threat, we first needed evidence that the stress response system had been activated relative to a resting baseline (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010).

text.text: We tested sympathetic activation in our samples by examining whether PEP shortened significantly from baseline for each time period (anticipation, conversation, and recovery).

text.text: Our primary hypothesis was that thoughts about stress (assessed via a self-reported challenge-threat index) collected in anticipation of a conversation would be positively associated with the body's response (assessed via a cardiovascular challenge-threat reactivity index) during the conversation.
This hypothesis was not supported in any study (see Table 3).

text.text: In additional exploratory analyses, we examined this association across all relevant timepoint pairings, and no significant effects were observed (see Table 3).

text.text: In Study 5, we did not find evidence that the selfreported indices of individuals who reported feeling more challenged than they typically felt during the conversation were associated with cardiovascular indices of greater challenge and less threat (i.e., no within-person effect; B = .02, SE = .03, t = 0.70, p = .487, r = .08, BF01 = 1.18e+12).
To further investigate these null findings, post-hoc Inclusion Bayes Factors were conducted (Clyde et al., 2011).
text.formatted: To further investigate these null findings, post-hoc Inclusion Bayes Factors were conducted <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Clyde et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: These Bayesian analyses allowed us to quantify the relative likelihood of the observed data being compatible with the null model vs. the alternative model when examining the association between self-reported and cardiovascular challenge-threat indices.

Specifically, we ran inclusion BF01 on the frequentist dyadic models, with the selfreported index included as a predictor of the cardiovascular index in the alternative model but not included in the null model.

Because we were comparing frequentist dyadic linear models with cardiovascular reactivity scores following an assumed normal distribution (Makowski et al., 2019), Bayes factors were approximated using the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) method (unit-information priors) with uniform-equal prior model odds (Faulkenberry, 2017), which were extracted using bayesfactor_inclusion() (Makowski et al., 2019) from nested gls() linear models (Pinheiro & Bates, 2000).
text.formatted: Because we were comparing frequentist dyadic linear models with cardiovascular reactivity scores following an assumed normal distribution <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Makowski et al., 2019)</ref>, Bayes factors were approximated using the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) method (unit-information priors) with uniform-equal prior model odds <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Faulkenberry, 2017)</ref>, which were extracted using bayesfactor_inclusion() <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Makowski et al., 2019)</ref> from nested gls() linear models <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Pinheiro & Bates, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Because the default prior settings in the bayesfactor_inclusion() function is a uniform-equal (i.e., flat) prior, we were not required to specify an explicit prior distribution for the parameters of either the null or alternative models.
This mitigates concerns regarding the selection of prior settings that would bias the analyses toward either the null or alternative hypothesis.

Although the BIC approximation is robust to prior choices, it is important to note that wider priors (i.e., prior distributions with greater variability) tend to favor the null hypothesis more strongly (Makowski et al., 2019).

Although combining resources and demands and CO and TPR reactivity into indices of challenge/threat is common in the field, our analytic approach may have obscured potential associations between self-reported and cardiovascular responses to stress.

We conducted robustness analyses in which we allowed anticipatory demands, resources, and their interaction to simultaneously predict CO and TPR reactivity during the conversation (see supplemental materials for additional details and OSF for data, code, and output).

The pattern of (null) results observed in primary analyses held when using this alternative approach -of the 30 possible tests, one was significant (3.33%) and in a direction inconsistent with the BPS-CT (greater selfreported demands was associated with greater CO; i.e., greater threat was associated with greater challenge).
Next, we explored whether the association between the self-reported and cardiovascular indices was moderated by the social context in which it was embedded.
Specifically, we tested an individual's role in the conversation as well as the type of conversation as potential moderators.
Across these analyses, the pattern of results did not change.
Thus, in the interest of brevity we fully report the results of these analyses in the supplemental materials for interested readers.

Although stress is broadly considered a "full-body experience" (e.g., McEwen, 2013; Blascovich & Mendes, 2001), we lack a comprehensive understanding of the extent to which the mind and body cohere in response to stressors.
text.formatted: Although stress is broadly considered a "full-body experience" (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">McEwen, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Blascovich & Mendes, 2001)</ref>, we lack a comprehensive understanding of the extent to which the mind and body cohere in response to stressors.

text.text: The aim of the current investigation was to examine this alignment through self-reported stress appraisals and cardiovascular reactivity.
Data were collected across five dyadic studies (N = 1,850) before, during, and after a social interaction.
Across all analyzed timepoint pairings, no significant association between the selfreported and cardiovascular challenge/threat indices was found.
Post-hoc Inclusion Bayes Factors provided support for the null (vs. alternative) hypothesis across all five studies.
Post-hoc mini meta-analyses suggest that this near-zero association may generalize beyond social interactions.
These findings challenge long-standing theoretical beliefs about stress and suggest that current methods of stress measurement may warrant critical re-evaluation.
Below, we outline three potential explanations for these results alongside associated avenues for future research.
First, it may be that the self-reported and cardiovascular indices each offer distinct, yet individually valid, windows into the stress response process.

A lack of association between these measures contradicts assumptions of the BPS-CT (that self-reported and cardiovascular measures each index the same underlying challenge/threat state), raising the question of whether the current framework is the best way to holistically model the stress response system.

If both indices demonstrate validity and reliability, and their null association continues to hold across contexts, future work must critically examine the BPS-CT in order to either reconcile these findings with the existing model or comprehensively amend the framework.
Well-established findings within the field of affective science could serve to guide this endeavor.
Emotions are commonly defined as a coordination of experience, behavior, and physiology, suggesting a degree of alignment between the mind and body (e.g., Ekman, 1992).
text.formatted: Emotions are commonly defined as a coordination of experience, behavior, and physiology, suggesting a degree of alignment between the mind and body (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Ekman, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Despite this, extant work examining agreement between these channels has found little support (Hollenstein & Lanteigne, 2014; Mauss et al., 2024), instead arguing that all three response channels are relevant to understanding emotion and that the construct cannot effectively be captured with any singular measure (Mauss & Robinson, 2009).
text.formatted: Despite this, extant work examining agreement between these channels has found little support <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hollenstein & Lanteigne, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Mauss et al., 2024)</ref>, instead arguing that all three response channels are relevant to understanding emotion and that the construct cannot effectively be captured with any singular measure <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Mauss & Robinson, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Adopting this perspective as it relates to the BPS-CT suggests that future work should aim to disentangle the conscious experience of stress from the body's response to stress rather than assuming that both self-reported and physiological indices tap into the same underlying state.
Continued efforts to refine and advance the BPS-CT would aid in mapping the stress response as a rich and complex "full-body" system.
Second, this pattern of results may be conceptualized as a lack of convergent validity between two leading measures of challenge and threat.
One of the indices may not be indexing the underlying challenge/threat states they are assumed to capture, thus impeding researchers seeking to examine these constructs.

The cardiovascular index draws upon fundamental anatomical principles and theoretically aligns with other well-established stress models that define stress responses through physiological patterns (McEwen, 1998; Dienstbier, 1989) and thus is an unlikely candidate for future refinement.
text.formatted: The cardiovascular index draws upon fundamental anatomical principles and theoretically aligns with other well-established stress models that define stress responses through physiological patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(McEwen, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Dienstbier, 1989)</ref> and thus is an unlikely candidate for future refinement.

text.text: However, the self-reported index (Mendes et al., 2007), while bolstered by evidence of the measures' validity (e.g., Peters et al., 2024; Beltzer et al., 2014; Jamieson et al., 2012) and reliability (ᾱ = .762, r2 DD = .822), is limited by its lack of formal scale development, identifying the need for a well-validated "gold standard" for selfreported challenge and threat.
text.formatted: However, the self-reported index <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Mendes et al., 2007)</ref>, while bolstered by evidence of the measures' validity (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Peters et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Beltzer et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Jamieson et al., 2012)</ref> and reliability (ᾱ = .762, r2 DD = .822), is limited by its lack of formal scale development, identifying the need for a well-validated "gold standard" for selfreported challenge and threat.

text.text: Alternatively, the BPS-CT consistently contends that evaluation of resources and demands is not an entirely conscious process (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010; Seery, 2011).
text.formatted: Alternatively, the BPS-CT consistently contends that evaluation of resources and demands is not an entirely conscious process <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Seery, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, it is possible that self-reported measures can only index one portion of a psychological appraisal process that could be further elucidated through implicit or behavioral measures.

Finally, future work that simultaneously examines the respective outcomes of selfreported and cardiovascular indices would allow researchers to articulate when these measures may meaningfully diverge in predicting downstream consequences of stress.

We hope these findings serve as a foundation for improving stress measurement as these developments would guide researchers in designing manipulations of challenge and threat, choosing appropriate measures to index challenge and threat responses, and making informed predictions regarding the outcomes of their challenge/threat indices.
Third, it is possible that the population and context assessed in the current work represent boundary conditions on the association of self-reported and cardiovascular indices.

Conclusions of the current work are limited by our sample of primarily White, female, college-aged individuals as some research suggests the degree of concordance between self-reported and cardiovascular measures may vary by population characteristics (Rith-Najarian et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Conclusions of the current work are limited by our sample of primarily White, female, college-aged individuals as some research suggests the degree of concordance between self-reported and cardiovascular measures may vary by population characteristics <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Rith-Najarian et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, the present work examined stress within social-evaluative interactions specifically, further limiting generalizability.

However, the reported mini meta-analyses do suggest that these findings generalize to athletic, cognitive, and performance-based tasks (see Table S10), with even the most conservative of these tests suggesting that only 0.7% of the variance in cardiovascular reactivity was explained by self-reports.
text.formatted: However, the reported mini meta-analyses do suggest that these findings generalize to athletic, cognitive, and performance-based tasks (see Table <ref type="table">S10</ref>), with even the most conservative of these tests suggesting that only 0.7% of the variance in cardiovascular reactivity was explained by self-reports.

text.text: As the association between self-reported and physiological indices of stress is rarely examined in the field (Hase et al., 2019), we encourage future work that aims to replicate and extend our findings across new contexts and populations.
text.formatted: As the association between self-reported and physiological indices of stress is rarely examined in the field <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hase et al., 2019)</ref>, we encourage future work that aims to replicate and extend our findings across new contexts and populations.

text.text: We leveraged a full-body theoretical account of stress through the BPS-CT to examine the association between individuals' conscious perceptions and physiological responses to stress.
Across multiple time points surrounding a variety of conversation tasks, we did not find evidence that thoughts about stress were associated with cardiovascular responses.
Mini meta-analytic evidence suggested that this mind-body disconnection may generalize beyond social interactions.
Together, results demonstrate a lack of convergence between two leading measures of challenge and threat, challenging fundamental tenets of the BPS-CT.

Although theories of stress often emphasize the mind-body connection, the current findings contribute to a growing body of literature identifying contexts in which the conscious experience of and bodily response to stress may be independent of one another.
Thus, to better understand stress as a "full-body experience", we advocate for a multi-method biopsychosocial approach to measuring stress and advancing theoretical models of stress responding.

text.text: Article searches were conducted in Google Scholar using two different approaches.

First, we screened all articles citing Quigley et al. (2002) or Tomaka et al. (1993), two publications that provided foundational evidence of an association between self-reported and cardiovascular measures of challenge and threat.
text.formatted: First, we screened all articles citing <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Quigley et al. (2002)</ref> or <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Tomaka et al. (1993)</ref>, two publications that provided foundational evidence of an association between self-reported and cardiovascular measures of challenge and threat.

text.text: The same process was used as new articles were found that interpreted and discussed the association between the two measurement types.
However, this strategy did not return articles that had simply reported a correlation without further mention.

Thus, we screened all articles containing the phrase "challenge and threat" authored by foundational researchers in the field (e.g., Blascovich, Berry-Mendes) as well as all other authors found in previous rounds of screening (i.e., for any author that had reported an association once, all additional articles on challenge and threat by that author were screened).

To be included, an article had to be peer-reviewed, contain at least one empirical work, and report at least one association between a self-reported measure of challenge and threat and one cardiovascular indicator of challenge and threat. 969 articles were screened, 38 reported an association (see Table S1), and 5 operationalized self-reported and cardiovascular indices consistent with the current work.

text.text: We report the results of the mini meta-analysis conducted on
ECG), impedance cardiography (ICG), and blood pressure (BP).
ECG electrodes (affixed in a lead II configuration) and ICG hardware (NICO100C, Biopac Systems, Inc.) measured impedance magnitude (Z0) and its derivative (dZ/dt).
Signals were sampled at 200 (Studies 1-3) or 1000 Hz (Studies 4-5), recorded using AcqKnowledge software, and integrated with a Biopac MP150 (Studies 1, 2, and 3) or MP160 (Studies 4 and 5) system.
BP readings (systolic, diastolic, and mean arterial pressure) were taken via a cuff placed on the participant's arm.
Readings were initiated and recorded in two-minute intervals through an ambulatory monitoring system in a separate room (ColinT105, Colin Medical Instruments, San Antonio, TX).
ECG and ICG signals were scored using MindWare software (v3.0.21, v.3.0.25, or 3.2.4; MindWare Technologies, Gahanna, OH) by trained research assistants unaware of the conditions of the study.
Scored in one-minute epochs, signals were analyzed for artifacts and ensemble averages were created.
The Mindware software placed B points in the dZ/dt wave (opening of aortic valve) and Q points in the ECG wave (start of left ventricle contraction) using the maximum slope change method.
R points of the ECG wave (left ventricle contraction) were also calculated using Mindware.
All B, Q, X, and R points created by Mindware were visually examined and manually adjusted by trained research assistants.
